title: Generating Characteristics (Table 3.3) & Distinctive Features (Table 3.4)
text:
All knights generate the five Characteristics the same way regardless of gender.
(Uses/derived values: see [[core.game-system.characteristics]].)

## Constructed method

**Distribute 60 points** among SIZ/DEX/STR/CON/APP, no final value below **8** or
above **15** (before the cultural modifier). **Cymric** characters then add the
**Cultural Characteristic Modifier of +3 CON**.

## Random method — Table 3.3 (Random Cymric Characteristic Values)

Roll as shown, then apply the Cymric **+3 CON** modifier.

| Characteristic | Roll | Cultural Maximum* |
|----------------|------|-------------------|
| SIZ | 2D6+5 | 18 |
| DEX | 2D6+5 | 18 |
| STR | 2D6+5 | 18 |
| CON | 2D6+5 | 21 |
| APP | 2D6+5 | 18 |

\*Cultural Maximum = the highest value reachable over the character's lifetime
through normal improvement.

> Advice: STR+SIZ ≥ 21 gives Damage 4D6 (≥ 27 gives 5D6); CON ≥ 11 for decent Hit
> Points. Low Characteristics can be reduced further by wounds/aging until bedridden.

### SIZ equivalents (reference)

Average weight/height per SIZ (±5 lb / ±1½"): SIZ 5 ≈ 62 lb / 4'3"; 8 ≈ 95 lb /
4'11"; 10 ≈ 125 lb / 5'5"; 12 ≈ 144 lb / 5'8"; 15 ≈ 177 lb / 6'1"; 18 ≈ 218 lb /
6'6"; 21 ≈ 268 lb / 7'; 25 ≈ 354 lb / 7'8".

## Table 3.4 — Distinctive Features (by APP)

APP sets an appearance category and how many Distinctive Features (chosen by the
player, GM approval; some may be **heritable**). Positive/negative feature word-lists
(Physique, Limbs, Hair, Face, Speech) are examples only.

| APP | Appearance | Features |
|-----|-----------|----------|
| 5 or less | Infirm | At death's door |
| 6–7 | Unseemly | Three negative |
| 8–9 | Ill-favored | Two negative |
| 10–12 | Plain | One negative, one positive |
| 13–15 | Fair | Two positive |
| 16–18 | Elegant | Three positive |
| 19 or more | Surpassing | Four positive |

title: Creation Methods, Culture/Gender/Name & Starting Religion (Table 3.2)
text:
## Three creation methods (pick one, don't cherry-pick)

- **Pregenerated** — copy a template from p.248, fill remaining details.
- **Constructed** — spend a fixed number of points as you choose (a character strong
  where you want, weaker elsewhere).
- **Random** — dice generate most Statistics; produces quirky, uneven characters.

## Personal information

Default assumptions: it is **508**, a **Cymric** knight of **Salisbury** (residing at
Sarum), lord is Robert, future Count of Salisbury; the PK is the designated heir of a
vassal knight. Core PKs are all **Cymric** (the most numerous, most play-advantaged
culture); other cultures/homelands live in supplements.

- **Gender** — knights may be **Sir** or **Dame** with **no mechanical difference**.
  Characteristics are generated identically regardless of gender. (See
  [[pendragon-gender-class-rule]].)
- **Name** — generally a single personal name; no surnames.

## Table 3.2 — Starting Religion (Random, roll 1D6)

Weighted toward a mostly-Christian population; GMs may adjust.

| 1D6 | Religion |
|-----|----------|
| 1–5 | Christian |
| 6 | Pagan |

Constructed method: simply **choose Christian or Pagan**.

> **No intelligence stat:** nothing quantifies intelligence/wisdom. Traits &
> Passions measure emotion, Characteristics the body, Skills specific cultural
> knowledge.

title: Ranks (Page/Squire/Knight) & Training and Practice
text:
## Ranks on the road to knighthood

- **Page** — boys and girls aged **7–14** learning courtly life. Most girls then
  become maids-in-waiting/wives; all boys and some girls become squires.
- **Squire** — serves a knight to learn knighthood. Those with promise, confidence,
  and connections may become knights; the rest usually stay squires past 21 and
  become **esquires** (not serving a specific knight). **All starting characters
  begin as squires on the cusp of knighthood.**
- **Knight** — most squires serve until **age 21** before knighting. Younger is
  exceptional (Lancelot at 18); a lord may hastily ennoble a young heir at **18** or,
  rarely, **15**.

## Qualifying for knighthood

A squire must be **at least 18** and have **value 10** in each of **Sword, Charge,
Brawling**, and **two non-weapon Knightly Skills** of choice (usually Horsemanship
and Courtesy). High Honor and Valorous are advisable but not required. A squire who
hasn't qualified by 21 begins play as an **esquire**. Players who wish to begin as
knights always may; the GM may allow slight Skill adjustments or an in-game
justification to qualify.

## Training & Practice (squire years)

For a first character, invest **up to 7 years** of Training & Practice (a modified
Winter Phase). **For each year of training, select one:**

- Distribute **5 points** among Skills (same limits as Personal Skill Additions —
  see [[core.character-creation.starting-skills]]).
- Add **1 point to any Trait** (max 19) **or Passion** (max 20).
- Add **1 point** to STR, SIZ, DEX, CON, or APP (this does **not** retroactively
  change beginning Skill values). No Characteristic may exceed its **Cultural
  Maximum**.

## Age & year born

Note age and year born: ask the GM the current game year and subtract your age. The
default starting age is **21**.

title: Parent's Glory, Inherited Glory & Quick Family History (Table 3.1)
text:
## Inherited Glory

At age 14 a character inherits **one-quarter of their knightly parent's Glory** (at
that time, or at the parent's death), up to an inherited maximum of **4,000 points**.
Every starting character thus begins with reflected Glory. If both parents are
knights, use the **higher** of the two Glory values.

To find the parent's Glory if unknown: either use the **Quick Family History**
below, or roll **6D6 × 100** and add **2,000** (for inherited Glory, knighting,
marriage, and title).

## Quick Family History

Assume the parent was born 462, squired 476, knighted & married 483, and their
eldest child (the PK) born 487. The parent starts with **(2D6×100) + 2,000** Glory.
By the time the PK turns 14 (in 501), the parent earned an **additional
(3D6×100) + 500** Glory. **For each full 500 of that additional Glory, roll once on
Table 3.1: Heroic Events.** These become family lore the PK can invoke for clout.

## Table 3.1 — Heroic Events (roll 1D6)

Entries marked * are rerolled if already held.

| 1D6 | Event |
|-----|-------|
| **1** | *Battle of Mount Damen* (484). Second roll: Rescued Count Roderick at the Battle of Eburacum.\* |
| **2** | *Battle of Lindsey* (490). Second roll: Participated in the capture of King Octa.\* |
| **3** | *Battle of St. Albans* (495). Second roll: Participated in the killing of King Octa.\* |
| **4** | **Saxon Raid** (498 + 1D6; roll 1D6): 1–3 destroyed a raiding group single-handed; 4 rescued a damsel, killing her kidnappers (family owes an **F2D3** Favor); 5 defeated a Saxon chieftain (gain a rune-scribed Saxon sword + an enemy in his son); 6 defeated a berserker (gain polished amber knob on a thong, worth £1). |
| **5** | **Variable Quest** (491/500; roll 1D6): 1 quested for Merlin (known to the Arch-Druid); 2 killed Djerl the Goblin and was cursed\*; 3 killed Jongon the Giant (surviving giants bear a grudge)\*; 4 killed Djell the Spriggan and was cursed\*; 5 escorted Princess Morgan to her wedding to King Uriens\*; 6 emissary to King Nanteleod of Escavalon\*. |
| **6** | **Variable Battle of…** (505–507; roll 1D6): 1 Terrabil (killing of Duke Gorlois); 2 Dorchester (hero in Dorset, hated by Cornishmen — heritable)\*; 3 Sarum (wounded King Cerdic, who escaped)\*; 4 Royston (killing of King Aescwine of Essex)\*; 5 Cambridge (wounded King Cwichelm, who escaped)\*; 6 Summerland (hero in Summerland, hated by Cornishmen — heritable)\*. |

By default a new knight receives the **best gear the family can afford**:

title: Starting Passions (Courts, Honor & Inherited Passions)
text:
**Passions** are intense beliefs that can inspire (boost a single Skill briefly). A
Passion over **15 compels** the character to act on it. Passions are grouped into
four **courts** — **Fidelitas, Fervor, Adoratio, Civilitas** — plus **Honor**, which
stands alone. **The total of all Passions in each court is capped at 40.** PKs start
with at least one Passion in each court:

- **Fidelitas:** **Homage (Lord)** (household knights) — *mercenaries take **Fealty**
  instead*.
- **Fervor:** **Love (Family)**, perhaps a **Hate**.
- **Adoratio:** **Devotion (Deity)**.
- **Civilitas:** **Station** and **Hospitality**.
- **Cultural Passions** (e.g. **Hate (Saxons)** for all Salisbury folk in the Boy
  King period).

A knight needs **Honor of at least 5** to qualify for their station and retain
knighthood. PKs pursuing an Ideal (Chivalry, Romance) should check Chapter 6.

## Constructed method

Start with **Honor** and **Homage (Lord)** at **15**; **Love (Family), Station,
Hospitality** at **10**; **Devotion (Deity)** at **5**. Salisbury PKs also get **Hate
(Saxons) at 5**. Distribute an extra **15 points** among these or other Passions. **No
Passion above 15** by this method.

## Random method

**Honor** and **Homage (Lord)** at **2D6+8**; **Love (Family), Hospitality, Station**
at **2D6+3**; **Devotion (Deity)** at **1D6+2**; Salisbury's **Hate (Saxons)** at
**1D6+2**. Distribute **no more than 4D6+1** further points. **No Passion above 15.**

## Inherited Passions (optional)

To pass a parent's Passion to their child: take the **parent's Passion value − 15**
and add that difference (**max +5**) as a bonus to the child's starting value. Use the
parent's value at the child's creation, or at the parent's death if earlier.

title: Starting Skills (Table 3.5 & 3.6) — Beginning Values, Cultural & Family bonuses
text:
Determine Skills in order: **Beginning Values → Cultural Skill Modifiers → Family
Characteristic → Personal Skill Additions.** Beginning values are set at age 14;
later Characteristic changes don't alter them.

## Table 3.5 — Beginning Knight Skill Values

Values shown as `APP−5`, `DEX/2`, or `STR/2` derive from that Characteristic.

| Skill | Begin | | Skill | Begin |
|-------|-------|-|-------|-------|
| Awareness\* | 5 | | Play Instrument | DEX/2 |
| Compose | 5 | | Recognize\* | 5 |
| Courtesy\* | APP−5 | | Religion | 5 |
| Dancing | DEX/2 | | Singing | 5 |
| Falconry | 5 | | Stewardship | 5 |
| Fashion | APP−5 | | **Battle\*** | 5 |
| First Aid\* | DEX/2 | | **Horsemanship\*** | DEX/2 |
| Flirting | APP−5 | | **Brawling\*** | STR/2 |
| Folklore | APP−5 | | **Charge\*** | DEX/2 |
| Gaming | 5 | | Hafted | DEX/2 |
| Hunting\* | 5 | | **Sword\*** | DEX/2 |
| Intrigue | APP−5 | | Spear | DEX/2 |
| Literacy | 0 | | Two-Handed Hafted | DEX/2 |
| Orate | APP−5 | | Bow / Crossbow / Thrown | DEX/2 |

\***Knightly Skills** — must reach **10** in Brawling, Charge, Sword, and **two**
non-weapon Knightly Skills of choice to qualify for knighthood.

## Cultural Skill Modifiers

**Cymric knights:** **+3 to Charge, Horsemanship, and Courtesy.**

## Table 3.6 — Family Characteristic (+3 to one Skill)

Every family shares one talent. **Constructed:** choose an entry (not "Gifted").
**Random:** roll 1D20.

| 1D20 | (Skill) | 1D20 | (Skill) |
|------|---------|------|---------|
| 1 Perceptive | Awareness | 11 Equestrian | Horsemanship |
| 2 Martial | Battle | 12 Scheming | Intrigue |
| 3 Poetic | Compose | 13 Silver-tongued | Orate |
| 4 Well-Bred | Courtesy | 14 Literate | Literacy (Language) |
| 5 Sprightly | Dancing | 15 Everyman | Folklore |
| 6 Seductive | Flirting | 16 Musical | Play Instrument |
| 7 Bird Lover | Falconry | 17 Devout | Religion |
| 8 Healer | First Aid | 18 Melodic | Singing |
| 9 Astute | Recognize | 19 Clodhopper | Stewardship |
| 10 Clever | Gaming | 20 **Gifted** | Roll twice more\* |

\*A second **20** = Transcendent Beauty (Involuntary Adoration, p.89); two 20s raise
the Adoration bonus to **+10**. Gifted bonuses are **not inherited** — offspring
reroll.

## Personal Skill Additions

Distribute **10 points** among Skills, with these limits:

- No Skill above **15** (including Cultural/Family bonuses).
- Cannot raise a Skill whose starting value is **0**.
- Except for Cultural/Family bonuses, APP-based Skills may not exceed the **APP**
  value at creation.
- **Horsemanship effectively caps mounted Weapon Skills** (see p.149).

title: Starting Personality Traits & Religious Virtues
text:
**Traits** guide a character's actions and come in **pairs summing to 20**, written
as `13/7`. As one rises the other falls. A character tends to act on the higher
Trait; a value of **16+** may dictate behavior even at inopportune moments (and
grants Glory). Full rules: **Chapter 4**.

**The 13 Trait pairs:** Chaste/Lustful, Energetic/Lazy, Forgiving/Vengeful,
Generous/Selfish, Honest/Deceitful, Just/Arbitrary, Merciful/Cruel, Modest/Proud,
Prudent/Reckless, Spiritual/Worldly, Temperate/Indulgent, Trusting/Suspicious,
Valorous/Cowardly.

## Religious Virtues (underline on sheet)

- **Christian:** Chaste, Forgiving, Merciful, Modest, Spiritual, Temperate
- **Pagan:** Lustful, Energetic, Generous, Honest, Proud, Spiritual

## Constructed method

- All Traits start at **10**.
- Raise the Traits your **religion favors to 13**.
- **Valorous always begins at 15** (martial training).
- Raise **one Trait to 16**.
- Distribute **6 points** freely (no Trait above 15 by this step).

## Random method

Roll **2D6+3** for each **left-hand** Trait, top to bottom — **except Valorous,
which is 2D6+8**. When you roll a **Religious Trait** for your faith (e.g. Energetic
for Christians — *note the book's example; Energetic is a Pagan virtue*), add **+3**;
when you roll the **opposite** of one of your religious virtues, subtract **−3**.
(Random values may exceed 15.)

**Fill in opposites:** each right-hand value = **20 − left-hand**; confirm every pair
sums to exactly 20.

title: Actions: Attack, Reckless Attack, Withhold Damage
text:
## Attack (Combat) — Mounted, Unmounted

The most common Action: try to damage the opponent with any Weapon Skill.
- **Distance:** Close Quarters, Normal, Long, Missile
- **Contest:** Weapon Skill vs. opponent's Action.

**Attacking a Horse or Weapon.** You may declare an attack on a rider's horse,
though this is dishonorable between knights (**−1 Honor**); a partial success by
the opponent lets the horse benefit from Shield/Parry Protection. Attacking a
horse from foot negates the −5 Height penalty, but the mounted opponent still
gets their +5 Height Advantage. You may instead target the opponent's **weapon**
to break it: the small target imposes **−5** to Weapon Skill, and a win breaks it
(a sword is knocked from the hand instead).

## Reckless Attack (Combat) — Mounted, Unmounted

An unguarded frenzy; always earns a **check to the Reckless trait**. Famously
Reckless characters must use it unless Prudent wins an opposed roll; Exemplary
Reckless must always use it. If one side Reckless-Attacks and the other Defends,
the two cancel and combat resolves normally.
- **Distance:** Close Quarters, Normal, Long
- **Contest:** Weapon Skill vs. opponent's Action; if the opponent is rolling a
  Weapon Skill they get **+5**. **Neither** side may apply Shield/Parry Protection.
- **Win:** deal **+2D6** Damage (**+6D6** on a critical).

## Withhold Damage (Combat) — Mounted, Unmounted

Deliberately reduce your strike: either withhold a preset number of dice, or use
the flat/butt for half damage (roll normal, halve). Using the flat every blow
dishonors the opponent (**−1 Honor** at end of combat). Only usable with a
normal Attack — never on a Mounted Charge or with thrown/missile weapons.
- **Distance:** Close, Normal, Long — **Contest:** Weapon Skill vs. opponent's Action.

title: Action: Call Squire
text:
Squires stay near their knights but may not be close enough to help immediately.
Declare **why** you are calling — usually one of: **First Aid** (heal wounds),
**New weapon** (brings a requested weapon; the knight re-arms), or **Fresh
horse** (brings a mount). Calling does not instantly accomplish the action —
e.g. First Aid needs the squire to pull the knight from combat and spend several
(**1D6**) minutes treating, possibly removing armor.
- **Distance:** Within hearing range
- **Contest:** None — make an unopposed **Squire Roll** (target = Squire Skill).

**Squire Roll Result:**
- **Critical:** squire acts and proceeds with the desired action **this round**.
- **Success:** squire acts and proceeds **next round**.
- **Fail:** squire does not act; the character may call again next round.
- **Fumble:** squire is nowhere to be seen; may reappear later at the GM's discretion.

title: Action: Disarm
text:
Disarm attempts to knock away the opponent's weapon or object from their grasp.
(Attempts to *wrench or seize and take* a weapon use the **Grapple** Action
instead.)
- **Distance:** Close Quarters, Normal
- **Contest:** Weapon Skill vs. opponent's Action
- **Critical:** the weapon/object flies out of easy reach, or lands at the
  character's feet (character's choice).
- **Win:** the opponent drops the weapon/object within reach; it may be picked up
  as a non-Combat action the following round. If more than one character tries to
  pick it up, resolve with an opposed DEX roll.

title: Action: Grapple, Follow-up Actions (Table 7.3) & Escape
text:
## Grapple (Brawling) — Mounted, Unmounted

A normally two-handed attempt to grab a foe or seize an object from their grip
(one-handed at **−5**). A foot character may Grapple a foe on foot or mounted,
but a mounted character may only Grapple another mounted foe. You may Grapple
**only one** foe at a time.
- **Distance:** Contact or Close Quarters
- **Contest:** Brawling vs. opponent's Action. **On a win, select a Follow-up
  Action from Table 7.3.**

## Follow-up Actions

A successful Grapple can be maintained into later rounds (no re-roll needed unless
the opponent attempts an Escape). Roll your normal Damage dice (**+2D6** on a
critical) and compare the total against the opponent's listed Characteristic/Skill
— the total must **exceed** the target for the action to take effect. This
"damage" ignores armor and normally inflicts no actual damage, **except** if the
roll is **≥ twice the target**, you also inflict your Brawling Damage (ignoring
armor).

**Table 7.3 — Follow-up Actions** (damage must exceed opponent's…):

| Action | Beat | Outcome | Grapple maintained? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disarm | Weapon Skill | Opponent drops weapon | Y |
| Hold | STR | Opponent pinned | Y |
| Lift | SIZ | Opponent lifted into the air | Y |
| Seize Weapon | Weapon Skill + ½ STR | Character takes opponent's weapon | N |
| Tackle | DEX | Opponent taken to the ground & pinned (mounted: 1D6 fall damage) | Y |
| Throw Down | SIZ | Must be Lifted first; thrown for 1D6 (foot) or 2D6 (horseback) damage | N |

Notes: a **Disarm** critical sends the weapon out of reach. A **pinned** opponent
(Hold/Tackle) may only attempt Escape, at **−10/+10**; the grappler may then use
any Follow-up automatically. SIZ ≥ 5× the opponent pins one-handed at no penalty;
SIZ < ⅕ the opponent cannot pin at all. A **Lifted** foe can be carried off
across a horse (lifting a foot foe from the saddle needs character+mount SIZ ≥
1½× the target). **Tackles** between mounted combatants require a Horsemanship
roll to avoid taking fall damage yourself.

## Escape (Act) — Unmounted

A pinned character may try to escape on later rounds: opposed roll of your
**Brawling −10** vs. the opponent's **Brawling +10**. Win → roll "damage" trying
to beat the grappler's STR. Lose → the opponent may execute a Follow-up Action as
normal.

title: Action: Hook
text:
Hook uses a bill, reversed longsword, or hooked farm implement (hoe, rake,
scythe) to snag an opponent and pull them to the ground.
- **Distance:** Any melee distance except Contact
- **Contest:** Weapon Skill vs. opponent's Action
- **Win:** inflict no damage; instead make an unopposed **STR roll** — on success
  it pulls the opponent down (ending the round on the ground) or unseats a rider
  (who takes **1D6** fall damage). On a **critical**, the opponent is
  automatically pulled down.

title: Action: Mounted Charge (+ Charge Opportunities, Lance Fumble Table 7.2)
text:
A Mounted Charge uses a weapon at full gallop. You must ride a combat-trained
horse capable of Charge Damage, not be engaged at the start of the round, and aim
at a specific opponent. Any weapon may be used except one causing Brawling
damage; spears and lances get special bonuses. The charge **must continue in a
Pass-by** regardless of hit or miss (see p. 149).

- **Distance:** Special — at least **six yards apart per charging character**.
- **Contest:** Charge vs. opponent's Action. **+5** if armed with a **couched**
  spear or lance against anyone not using a Long-reach weapon. For any other
  weapon, effective Charge Skill is the **lower** of Charge or the relevant
  Weapon Skill; and effective Charge Skill can **never exceed Horsemanship**.

**Results** (in addition to / instead of Table 7.1):
- **Win:** hit for Weapon Damage **+1D6**, or the horse's **Charge Damage** if
  using a couched spear/lance. Except on a critical, damage dice may not exceed
  the horse's Charge Damage. A critical adds **+4D6**.
- **Partial Success:** a spear, lance, or hafted weapon breaks.
- **Tie:** hafted weapon breaks; if both critical, the horses crash, each taking
  the other's Charge Damage.
- **Fumble:** sword dropped / hafted weapon breaks; a couched spear or lance also
  breaks **and** triggers a Horsemanship roll on **Table 7.2**.

**Charge Opportunities** (large melee, not engaged at round start): roll 1D6 —
**1–3** may Charge a random opponent (if that opponent is also mounted on a
combat horse, roll again to see if they also Charge); **4–6** no opportunity
(engage in normal melee instead).

**Table 7.2 — Mounted Lance Charge Fumble** (roll Horsemanship):
- **Critical:** lance broken; no further ill effects.
- **Success:** lance broken; struck by flying splinters for **1D6** (armor does
  not protect).
- **Failure:** tip buries in the earth and launches you from the saddle; lance
  broken, **2D6** damage (armor does not protect).
- **Fumble:** tip buries and brings down both you and horse; lance broken,
  **3D6** damage (armor does not protect).

title: Action: Self-sacrifice
text:
A Player may declare a Self-sacrifice for the common good (**GM approval
required** to prevent petty use or the loss of key characters like King Arthur).
The player describes their objective and desired outcome, which **succeeds
automatically** — no dice. In return, **the character dies at the end of the
action** and receives **1,000 Glory** for a heroic death, plus normal Glory for
deeds later witnessed or verified.

Limitations:
- It is not carte blanche — the GM maintains drama (e.g. a knight holding a
  bridge buys time, but not enough for the others to leisurely stroll away). The
  GM decides how long pursuers are delayed and need not tell the players.
- Against a **gargantuan** enemy (dragon, huge giant) a kill is **not
  guaranteed**: instead the hero does the equivalent of a **critical success with
  maximum damage, bypassing the foe's armor** (e.g. 4D6 +4D6 crit at max = 48
  points).

title: Action: Set Spear
text:
Set Spear counters a declared or potential **Charge** attack. The character sets
the butt of the spear against or into the ground, angled at the opponent or their
mount. The spear may be one- or two-handed: one hand allows use of a shield;
a **two-handed grip adds +2D6 damage**.

This Action **only works against an opponent using the Charge Skill** — otherwise
it counts as a simple Attack.
- **Distance:** Long
- **Contest:** Spear Skill vs. opponent's Action

title: Action: Trample
text:
Riders of combat-trained horses may Trample **prone** opponents within their
Movement Rate. Even Chivalrous knights may use it in the heat of battle, at least
against armed foes. Horses dislike stepping on objects, which **cancels the
rider's Height bonus** (though the opponent still suffers a penalty).
- **Distance:** Normal
- **Contest:** Horsemanship vs. opponent's Action **−5**
- **Win:** opponent takes a wound using the horse's **normal (non-Charging)
  Damage** (see Table 10.2: Combat Horses).

title: Action: Zigzag
text:
Zigzag is an evasive Action used while moving, effective **only against missile
attacks** (use Dodge for melee). A combatant wearing **no armor gets +5**. You
cannot Zigzag while moving faster than Walking pace.
- **Distance:** Missile
- **Contest:** unopposed Movement Rate roll, made **before** the missile attack.
- **Critical:** opponent takes **−10** to Missile Weapon Skill; you move up to
  full Movement Rate.
- **Success:** opponent takes **−5**; you move up to half Movement Rate.
- **Failure:** no modifier; you move up to half Movement Rate.
- **Fumble:** no modifier; you stumble and lose all Movement Rate this round.

title: Combat Actions — Overview & Classifications
text:
A **Combat Action** is anything a character chooses to do during a Combat Round.
The list below is the most common options; Gamemasters should ad-lib new ones
using these as a model.

**Action classifications:**

- **Act** — a non-Combat action (often a Characteristic or non-Combat Skill
  roll) that affects combat but does not damage the opponent.
- **Brawling** — damages/affects an opponent at Contact or Close Quarters,
  unarmed or with small/improvised weapons.
- **Combat** — damages/affects an opponent at Close Quarters or greater distance.
- **Communication** — conveys information; usually no die roll.
- **Follow-up Action** — triggered by a successful Grapple.

**Actions list:**

- *Mounted or Unmounted:* Attack, Call Squire, Claim a Prisoner, Defend, Disarm,
  Evade, Mount Up, Pick Up, Reckless Attack, Self-sacrifice, Study, Withhold
  Damage, Zigzag
- *Exclusively Unmounted:* Dodge, Don Armor, Hook, Set Spear
- *Exclusively Mounted:* Control Mount, Mounted Charge, Trample
- *Brawling:* Barehand Attack, Escape, Grapple, Slam

Each definition lists a **Distance** and a **Contest**; a **Results** subheading
appears only when outcomes differ from Table 7.1.

title: Brawling: Barehand Attack & Slam
text:
**Brawling Skill** applies whenever a character fights unarmed or with an
improvised weapon (e.g. a musical instrument) or small weapon (knife, dagger). It
always inflicts the character's **Brawling Damage**, though the weapon/object may
modify this. Brawling also covers grapples, slams, and escapes (see separate
entries).

## Barehand Attack (Brawling) — Mounted, Unmounted

Functions like Attack but uses the **Brawling Skill** instead of a Weapon Skill;
also used for daggers/improvised weapons. Unarmed strikes are a **punch** (closed
fist) or **slap** (open hand).
- **Distance:** Contact or Close Quarters
- **Contest:** Brawling vs. opponent's Action
- **Win:** Brawling Damage for a punch/brawling weapon, or half for a slap; a
  **critical adds +2D6**. Weapons inflict Brawling Damage + their bonus, and add
  the normal **+4D6** on a critical.
- **Fumble:** stumble (**−5** next round); improvised/wooden weapons break;
  daggers are dropped.

## Slam (Brawling) — Unmounted

Hurl your mass into an opponent at speed. Both combatants must be on foot. A foe
with the right weapon may respond with **Set Spear** if they see it coming from
Long distance.
- **Distance:** Close Quarters (**−5**), Normal, or Long (**+5**). Using a shield
  adds **+5**.
- **Contest:** Brawling vs. opponent's Action
- **Win:** roll damage normally (crit **+4D6**) but apply only **Brawling Damage**
  as a wound (armor protects normally). If total damage rolled **> opponent's
  SIZ**, both fall; if **> twice SIZ**, only the opponent is knocked prone.

title: Charge Distance
text:
An effective charge requires a minimum distance of **six yards** between
character and opponent to build enough deadly speed and momentum. A character
and opponent who are **charging each other** must start at least **twelve yards**
apart.

The maximum distance for a Mounted Charge is the horse's Movement Rate, at a
gallop, in one Combat Round. See *Chapter 10: Horses* for the Movement Rates of
horses and other mounts.

title: Combat Modifiers
text:
Circumstances apply bonuses or penalties. Against a single foe all modifiers
always apply; against multiple foes, different modifiers may apply per opponent.
**All modifiers are cumulative.**

- **Cover** — an obstacle (tree, bush, low wall) partially protecting a character
  in melee gives **both** combatants **−5**.
- **Height Advantage** — fighting from height (horseman vs. foot, rampart vs.
  climber, standing vs. prone) gives a **+5/−5 reflexive** modifier in the taller
  combatant's favor. Negated if an unmounted combatant uses a two-handed spear or
  halberd against a mounted foe. A mounted combatant using any weapon **except a
  spear cannot strike a prone opponent**. Missile attacks do not benefit.
- **Strike from Behind** — when the opponent doesn't know an attack is coming:
  an unopposed Attack at **+5** (usually dishonorable; may cost Honor).
- **Immobile Target** — grappled, entangled, stuck, etc.: **−10/+10 reflexive**
  to all actions needing freedom of movement.
- **Surprise** — a wholly unprepared opponent grants the attacker **+5** to
  Weapon Skill for the first round. A missile attack from Surprise ignores the
  target's shield penalty.
- **Visibility** — darkness, fog, or smoke penalizes all Combat Actions (see the
  Awareness skill, p. 98).

title: Combat Movement (Step Five)
text:
Characters who declared movement **other than a charge** now simultaneously move
up to their Movement Rate in yards. A character need not move their full rate,
but **once they choose to stop, they cannot move further** that round.

Movement decides whether a character has closed with an enemy so they may
engage. Once two combatants are within one yard of each other, melee combat is
possible. Except for charges, **all movement takes place at the end of the
Combat Round**.

title: The Combat Round
text:
The **Combat Round** is the basic time measure for single or small-group combat:
a short, elastic unit — the time to conceive of and perform one action in melee.
Rounds continue in succession until everyone is done fighting (through
incapacitation, death, surrender, or flight).

Each character is limited to **one action per round**. This is a loose limit: a
round is not merely a single blow but an exchange of attacks, parries, and
maneuvering. A roll made as a *reaction* to another (e.g. the DEX roll when your
Knockdown value is exceeded) is a **free action** and does not count as your
action for the round.

**Combat Round procedure** — both combatants simultaneously follow, each round:

1. **Declare Combat Actions**
2. **Resolve Combat Actions**
3. **Winner's Outcome**
4. **Loser's Outcome**
5. **Combat Movement**

**Step One — Declare.** All combatants state what they intend to do, the weapon
they wield, and their targets/opponents. Combatants within one yard of each
other are automatically **engaged** and need not move to fight. If timing
matters (e.g. one sets a spear while the other makes a Mounted Charge), resolve
conflicting declarations with opposed DEX rolls — declarations are made from
**lowest DEX to highest**, and the winner resolves first in Step Two.

**Step Two — Resolve.** Any Skill/Combat Skill resolution is made now.
Characters can either fight *or* move, not both — except a **Mounted Charge**,
which combines movement and attack and is resolved here (splitting into two
actions halves the Skill used in each). If combat occurs, both combatants roll
their modified Combat Skills using opposed resolution and consult **Table 7.1:
Combat Action Resolution Results**. Some actions (e.g. Dodge, Disarm) supersede
that table, as noted in the action's definition.

title: Damage & Wounds (Loser's Outcome)
text:
Record damage taken (after subtracting Protection) in the Wounds section of the
character sheet and subtract it from Total Hit Points. Note each wound
**separately** — First Aid is applied to each individually — and check what type
was inflicted (Minor, Major, or Mortal).

- **Major Wound:** if actual damage **equals or exceeds the loser's CON**, they
  suffer a Major Wound and fall unconscious.
- **Unconscious:** if Current Hit Points fall **below the Unconscious
  Characteristic**, the loser falls unconscious. They are out of the fight until
  First Aid raises Current Hit Points to at least their Unconscious value.
- **Mortally Wounded:** if Hit Points drop to **0 or less**, the character will
  die if not quickly rescued.

If **mounted** when knocked unconscious or Major-Wounded, the character may
attempt an **Emergency Dismount** (unopposed DEX roll): success = a gentle fall
doing little or no damage; failure = a bad fall causing **1D6** damage.

See *Chapter 11: Injury and Health* for wound effects and recovery.

title: Actions: Defend, Dodge, Evade
text:
## Defend (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

Forgo damage in favor of protecting yourself. A smart choice against
overwhelming odds.
- **Distance:** Any melee distance
- **Contest:** Weapon Skill **+10** vs. opponent's Action
- **Win or Tie:** take no damage, deal no damage.

## Dodge (Act) — Unmounted

Throw yourself aside to avoid damage. Your single roll is pitted against **all**
opponents' rolls and forgoes the usual multiple-opponents penalty. Usable at any
distance against melee attacks, but you must be on your feet. **Melee only — use
Zigzag for missiles.**
- **Distance:** Any melee distance
- **Contest:** Movement Rate vs. opponent's Action
- **Critical:** avoid damage, deal none, and begin next round ready to act.
- **Win:** avoid damage, deal none, but start next round on the ground (weapon
  still in hand).
- **Lose:** take all damage; start next round on the ground (weapon in hand).
- **Fumble:** take all damage, fall, start on the ground next round having
  dropped your weapon.

## Evade (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

Disengage from melee. Like Dodge, negates and deals no damage, and also carries
you **away** from combat.
- **Distance:** Any melee distance
- **Contest:** Movement Rate (horse's, if mounted) vs. opponent's Action
- **Win:** neither take nor deal damage; no longer engaged.
- **Fumble:** fall, start next round on the ground; if mounted, fall from the
  horse and take **1D6** damage.

title: Dropped or Broken Weapon
text:
A loser who **fumbles** their opposed weapon roll drops their sword or breaks
their non-sword weapon; the unfortunate character must start the next round
unarmed.

- **Swords** break all non-sword weapons other than daggers **on a tie**.
- A sword breaks **any** weapon, including another sword, when the loser fumbles
  and the winner criticals.

title: Example: Full Combat (worked example — pointer)
text:
A multi-round worked example (Sir Clydno ambushed by a gang of robbers while
mounted) demonstrating how actions and modifiers interact: Passion rolls
(Impassioned +10), Mounted Charge against multiple foes, the on-foot-vs-mounted
−5 penalty, Height Advantage, and Multiple Opponent penalties.

Not transcribed here — this is narrative illustration rather than rules. Consult
the Core Rulebook pp. 153–158 directly if you need the step-by-step walkthrough.
The mechanics it exercises are captured in [[core.combat.combat-round]],
[[core.combat.multiple-opponents]], [[core.combat.combat-modifiers]], and
[[core.combat.action-mounted-charge]].

title: Determining Knockdown
text:
Whenever a character takes a blow (from a weapon or another source, such as
riding into a tree limb), the **base damage** — damage before armor, rebated
weapons, or other reductions — is compared to their **Knockdown value**, which
equals their **SIZ** Characteristic.

- If damage received is **greater than Knockdown**, the character makes an
  unopposed **DEX roll** (whether on foot or mounted); multiple knockdowns in a
  round each require their own roll.
  - **Critical or success:** stays upright / in the saddle, no penalty.
  - **Failure or fumble:** knocked down — begins next round on the ground. If
    mounted, suffers **1D6** damage from the fall and drops their weapon.
- If damage is **greater than twice Knockdown**, the character is
  **automatically** knocked down (mounted: fall, 1D6 damage, drop weapon).
- If damage is **greater than the horse's SIZ**, the horse may be knocked down
  too — see "Horse and Rider Knocked Down" (p. 150).

title: Melee Distances
text:
Distances in melee vary according to the positions of combatants and their
weapons. Some actions require sustained physical contact, some weapons are only
effective at close quarters, and some weapons are so long they are effective
outside of normal melee distances.

Distances are expressed as one of **five qualitative categories**: Contact,
Close Quarters, Normal, Long, and Missile.

Characters may declare at which distance they wish to engage their opponent as
part of their action declaration; otherwise the Gamemaster determines it. When
combatants are within one yard's distance of each other, melee combat is
possible. To avoid combat and move past the enemy, Evasion may be necessary.

title: Missile Distances
text:
Missile ranges are:

- **Short** — up to 30 yards
- **Medium** — 31 to 100 yards
- **Long** — 101 to 200 yards

See "Missile Ranges" (p. 152) for additional rules.

title: Missile Weapons (ranges, modifiers, closing distance)
text:
Knights consider using missile weapons against other knights **cowardly** — a
knight gets a **Cowardly check and loses 1 Honor** for using a bow or crossbow
against another knight in single combat. (Crossbows in a besieged garrison are
acceptable.)

**Missile Ranges & penalties:**
- **Short** — up to 30 yards; the max range for all thrown weapons except javelins.
- **Medium** — 31–100 yards; **−5** to Weapon Skill; max range for javelins.
- **Long** — 101–200 yards; **−10** to Weapon Skill.

**Shielded Targets.** A shield-bearer aware of being targeted imposes the
shield's **Missile Attack Penalty** (e.g. kite shield **−10**) on the archer. The
archer may apply it to shots at the **mount** instead, but loses their own
shield's benefit that round. Shield/Parry Protection points otherwise do not
apply to missile fire.

**Cover** (targets on foot behind cover): Light **−5** (brush, moderate rocks),
Moderate **−10** (low wall, dense trees), Significant **−15** (arrow slit).

**Other Modifiers:** stationary opponents reduce range penalties by 5; Zigzag
**−5** (or **−10**); Surprise **+5**; wind — light 0, irregular **−5**, strong
constant **−10** (wind does not affect hand-hurled weapons).

**Closing Distance (Table 7.5)** — rounds to cross each band; compare to the
weapon's rate of discharge for shots before the attacker arrives. Zigzagging
attackers always use Walking Rate.

| Pace | Short (≤30) | Medium (31–100) | Long (101–200) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Walking | 2 | 4 | 6 |
| Jogging | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| Running | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Walk (mount) | 2 | 4 | 6 |
| Trot | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Canter | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Gallop | 1 | 1 | 1 |

**Other considerations:** *Loosing into a Melee* — equal chance to hit every
combatant; the GM assigns the target at random. *Mounted Targets* — roll 1D6:
**1–4** hits the mount, **5–6** the rider. *Visibility* — adverse conditions may
require an Awareness roll to see the target before shooting. *Water* — a wet bow
or crossbow gives **−5** Weapon Skill, **doubles** all effective ranges, and
**halves** damage.

title: Mounted Combat
text:
Pendragon centers on the mounted knight. See also the Control Mount, Mount Up,
Mounted Charge, Trample, and Zigzag actions.

**Horsemanship Limitation.** Horsemanship limits the **base value** of all Weapon
Skills used while riding; modifiers (combat, Passions, etc.) still apply and can
push the effective value back above Horsemanship. *E.g. Sword 17 with
Horsemanship 15 → effective 15 while mounted; a +5 mounted-vs-foot modifier then
raises it to 20 against that foe.*

**Pass-by.** A Mounted Charge always overshoots the target by a Pass-by distance
(the horse's motion after impact). Minimum distance to rein in = **half** the
horse's normal Movement Rate (the rider may circle to start next round in Normal
range); maximum = the horse's **gallop** Movement Rate minus the distance to
reach the target. On a Win or mutual miss the rider sets the distance; on a Tie
(double success), Partial, or Loss the maximum is **halved and the rider must go
the full distance**. A dismounted rider's horse gallops on for the maximum; if
the horse is knocked down or falls, no Pass-by occurs.

**Mounted Knockdown.** Normal Knockdown rules apply: total damage over SIZ → DEX
roll to stay in the saddle; over **twice SIZ** → automatically thrown. Falling
from the saddle causes **1D6** damage.

**Horse and Rider Knocked Down.** If total damage to *either* horse or rider
exceeds the **horse's SIZ**, the horse makes a DEX roll to stay standing; failure
knocks it down. The rider may attempt an Emergency Dismount; if that also fails,
the rider is **crushed** by the falling steed for the horse's normal Damage
(armor protects normally).

**Emergency Dismount** (unopposed Horsemanship roll — **Table 7.4**):
- **Critical:** land on feet, upright next round, no damage, keep all weapons.
- **Success:** land on feet, upright next round, no damage, but **drop** held weapons.
- **Failure:** improper dismount, **1D6** damage, drop all weapons.
- **Fumble:** **2D6** damage, drop all weapons; if the horse fell, it lands on
  the rider for the horse's Damage.

**Escaping from Under a Fallen Horse.** Each round roll the rider's **STR vs. the
horse's SIZ**; each helper adds +5 to the strongest person's STR (who rolls).

**Limited Two-handed Mounted Weapons.** From horseback, only a **longsword** and
a **two-handed spear** may be used two-handed; other two-handed weapons are too
unbalanced and risk unhorsing the rider.

**Too Big for Your Horse.** Compare the horse's STR to the rider's **SIZ×2**
(subtract 5 if unarmored). If that total exceeds the horse's STR: **−5**
Horsemanship, **−5** horse Movement Rate, treated as Forced March on long travel,
and horse Damage **−1D6**. If the rider's SIZ equals the horse's STR, the horse
cannot bear them at all.

title: Actions: Control Mount, Mount Up
text:
## Control Mount (Act) — Mounted

Get an unruly mount under control before another Action. See "Controlling Horses
in Combat" (p. 181).
- **Contest:** Unopposed Horsemanship roll (**−5** for non-combat-trained horses;
  further penalty equal to Hit Points the horse has lost to wounds).

A horse not trained for combat (any from Table 10.3: Riding Horses) forces a
Horsemanship roll at **−5** at the start of each round: **success** = control +
another action this round; **critical** = controlled for the rest of combat
unless wounded; **failure** = no other action this round; **fumble** = thrown,
must make an Emergency Dismount (p. 150). When any horse takes **5+ points** of
damage in a round, check injury effects; thereafter roll Horsemanship each round
(penalty = total HP lost) before acting — a combat-trained horse settles on a
critical *or* regular success.

## Mount Up (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

Takes one Combat Round to mount/dismount, unless a squire holds the reins, or you
roll Movement Rate (capped by Horsemanship) to leap into/out of the saddle and
act the same round. Mounting under blows uses an opposed roll (capped by
Horsemanship) vs. the opponent's Action.
- **Win:** mount up, take no damage.
- **Partial Success:** mount up but take damage; no shield/parry protection.
- **Loss:** remain unmounted and take damage; no shield/parry protection.
- **Fumble:** fall; start next round on the ground.

title: Multiple Opponents & Modifier Stacking
text:
Up to **three unmounted** (or **two mounted**) characters may attack one
opponent, since horses take up more space. A character facing several foes must
perform the **same action** against each and applies the Multiple Opponent
modifier separately per action.

**Multiple Opponent Modifier:** a cumulative **−5 per opponent after the first**
(two foes = −5 each; three = −10). Each action is resolved separately. A
character may instead **ignore** one or more opponents — each ignored opponent
gets an unopposed action, but imposes no −5.

**Charging Multiple Opponents** (GM approval): a Mounted Charge may hit several
close foes if they are all within the horse's gallop Movement Rate, in a roughly
straight line, each making an opposed roll, and the weapon isn't broken (a broken
weapon ends the run). The Multiple Opponent modifier applies to all rolls, with
**no cap** on targets.

**Modifier order:** apply **Personal Modifiers** first (they form the base the
Multiple Opponent modifier acts on) — these are **+10 from Defend** and magical
effects. Then apply the Multiple Opponent modifier. Then apply **Situational
Modifiers** (all Combat Modifiers, and Passion modifiers), which affect only the
specific opponent being fought.

title: Armor, Shield, and Parry Protection
text:
Armor and shields absorb damage; parries block it. All are expressed as a
**Protection value**.

The actual damage the loser takes is the difference between the **winner's
damage total** and the loser's **Armor Protection value**.

If the loser rolled a **partial success**, they may *also* apply the **Shield or
Parry Protection value** of their shield/weapon on top of Armor.

title: Re-Arming
text:
In combat, shafts are shattered and swords are dropped on a regular basis. How
long it takes to re-arm is circumstantial and subject to the Gamemaster's
ruling, but here are some guidelines:

- A character with a **sheathed sword or dagger** at their side may draw it at
  the start of a Combat Round without penalty. Weapons in any other location
  (strapped across the back, hung from a saddle or belt, etc.) impose a **−5
  penalty** to your Combat Action that round.
- Characters **on foot** may retrieve a dropped weapon within easy reach; this
  takes a Combat Action and may be opposed (see "Pick Up", p. 141).
- **Mounted** characters who drop a weapon may not retrieve it without
  dismounting first.

Re-arming with a weapon brought forth by your squire requires the **"Call
Squire"** Action (p. 138). You may drop any weapon or shield without taking a
Combat Action — so a knight who charges with their lance on the first round may,
at the start of the second round, drop the lance, draw their sword, and still
Attack.

title: Table 7.1 — Combat Action Resolution Results
text:
Both combatants roll their modified Combat Skill (opposed). Cross-reference the
character's result (rows) against the opponent's result (columns). "+4D6" marks
a critical, which adds a flat +4D6 to the winner's Damage. "no Shield/Parry"
means only Armor Protection applies (the loser did not achieve a partial
success). Damage is always reduced by the defender's Protection value.

| Character ↓ / Opponent → | **Critical** | **Success** | **Partial** | **Fail** | **Fumble** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | Tie: both suffer (Damage − Armor + Shield/Parry) | n/a | Char wins: opp suffers +4D6 − Armor + Shield/Parry | Char wins: opp suffers +4D6 − Armor (no Shield/Parry) | Char wins: opp suffers +4D6 − Armor (no S/P) **& drops/breaks weapon** |
| **Success** | n/a | Tie: both suffer (Damage − Armor + Shield/Parry) | Char wins: opp suffers Damage − Armor + Shield/Parry | Char wins: opp suffers Damage − Armor (no S/P) | Char wins: opp suffers Damage − Armor (no S/P) **& drops/breaks weapon** |
| **Partial** | Opp wins: char suffers +4D6 − Armor + Shield/Parry | Opp wins: char suffers Damage − Armor + Shield/Parry | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| **Fail** | Opp wins: char suffers +4D6 − Armor (no S/P) | Opp wins: char suffers Damage − Armor (no S/P) | n/a | Both lose: neither suffers Damage | Both lose: neither suffers Damage; **opp drops/breaks weapon** |
| **Fumble** | Opp wins: char suffers +4D6 − Armor (no S/P) **& char drops/breaks weapon** | Opp wins: char suffers Damage − Armor (no S/P) **& char drops/breaks weapon** | n/a | Both lose: neither suffers Damage; **char drops/breaks weapon** | Both lose: neither suffers Damage; **both drop/break weapon** |

The winner then resolves **Step Three: Winner's Outcome** — rolling Damage dice
equal to their Damage Characteristic (a critical adds +4D6).

title: Actions: Claim a Prisoner, Pick Up, Don Armor, Study
text:
## Claim a Prisoner (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

It takes a full Combat Round to accept a foe's surrender, during which you may
take no other action.

## Pick Up (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

Retrieve something within reach not worn by/attached to another person or object.
Use your hands, or use a spear/lance to pick up small objects from horseback.
- **Distance:** Contact, Close Quarters, Normal
- **Contest:** Unopposed = automatic success; if opposed, roll **DEX+5** vs.
  opponent's Action.

## Don Armor (Act) — Unmounted

Putting on armor takes more than one round; the time depends on armor type and
whether a squire/knight assists (see "Armoring Up", p. 169). Each round donning
armor must be devoted to nothing else. If forced to fight before finishing, you
count as **unarmored**.

## Study (Act) — Mounted, Unmounted

Look over the combat area to see who is prone, wounded, or faring well; the GM
describes the scene, with more detail the more rounds you spend. Obscured things
may require an immediate Awareness roll (with penalties). If attacked while
Studying, you may cancel it for another Action at **−5** for the first round.

title: Winner's Outcome
text:
In an opposed melee exchange, the combatant with the higher **successful** roll
is the winner and resolves their outcome first.

**Step Three: Winner's Outcome.** The winner rolls a number of dice equal to
their Damage Characteristic. A **critical success adds a flat +4D6** to the
Damage for that round (e.g. 5D6 becomes 5D6+4D6). Armor Points (plus any shield)
are subtracted from the total; the remainder is applied to the loser's Hit
Points.

**Step Four: Loser's Outcome.** The loser takes the winner's damage, and then:

- **Critical or success:** the loser stays mounted / keeps their footing.
- **Failure or fumble:** the loser is knocked down.

A loser who **fumbles** their opposed weapon roll may have their weapon broken:
swords break all non-sword weapons other than daggers on a tie.

title: Characteristics (SIZ, DEX, STR, CON, APP) & Derived values
text:
Five **Characteristics** quantify a character's physical qualities and generate a
set of **Derived Characteristics**. Characteristic rolls are simple **unopposed**
resolutions with **no critical/fumble effects and no experience checks**; they may
carry a modifier (usually environmental).

## The five Characteristics

- **SIZ (Size)** — a GM may set a SIZ value on a tight passage that too-large
  knights cannot pass; an opposed SIZ roll is needed to hurl/budge any object
  larger than ¼ of your SIZ. Also the **Knockdown** value (see
  [[core.combat.knockdown]]).
- **DEX (Dexterity)** — climbing, sneaking, swimming, balancing, throwing; keeps
  you upright/horsed; sets initial weapon Skill values; some Combat Actions need a
  DEX roll.
- **STR (Strength)** — feats of raw power (break doors, lift, pull people from
  under fallen horses), often via Fixed Opposition.
- **CON (Constitution)** — resist poisons/diseases, hold breath, onerous tasks (see
  Ch.11).
- **APP (Appeal)** — non-verbal impression (bearing, voice, symmetry); sets some
  social Skill values and matters at feasts. A knight in armor with a closed helm
  has virtually **no APP** (gender not even tellable). Severe disfigurement (from
  wilderness wandering or Madness) imposes **−10 to others' Recognize**, and Glory
  does not aid the Recognize Skill unless the coat of arms is displayed.

## Derived Characteristics

| Derived value | Formula |
|---------------|---------|
| **Knockdown** | = SIZ |
| **Major Wound** | = CON |
| **Total Hit Points** | = CON + SIZ |
| **Unconscious** | = Total Hit Points ÷ 4 |
| **Healing Rate** | = CON ÷ 5 |
| **Weapon Damage** (dice) | = (STR + SIZ) ÷ 6, in d6 |
| **Brawling Damage** (flat) | = (STR + SIZ) ÷ 6, as a flat number |
| **Movement Rate** | = (STR + DEX) ÷ 2, + 5 |

title: Core Concepts & Dice (Statistics, Values, Roll vs Check)
text:
## Statistics & Values

A **Statistic** quantifies a character quality and always has a numerical
**value**. Characteristics, Traits, Passions, Skills, Glory, and Armor / Parry /
Shield Protection are all Statistics. Values run on a scale of **1–20 (or more)**
and are recorded next to the Statistic (e.g. *Valorous 16, Sword 15*). A value may
rise or fall over time or be temporarily modified for a single roll.

### Trait & Passion value ranges

Trait and Passion values fall into qualitative bands:

| Band | Value | Meaning |
|------|-------|---------|
| **Unsung** | 0–4 | Never known for it; does not define personality |
| **Normal** | 5–15 | Defines personality more as it nears 15 |
| **Famous** | 16–20 | Well-known for it, at least within their home county |
| **Exalted** | 20 (+x) | A critical bonus over 20; completely defines them, known everywhere |

## Dice

Pendragon uses only **d6** and **d20**. The d20 determines success or failure for
**all Statistic tests**; d6s handle damage and other randomized outcomes. Roll all
needed dice together when possible.

Notation:

- **D** — number and type of dice: the number left of the D is how many dice, the
  number right is how many sides. `5D6` = five six-sided dice.
- **1D20** — a single twenty-sided die.
- **1D3** — roll a d6 where 1–2 = 1, 3–4 = 2, 5–6 = 3.
- **+x** — a fixed number added to a result (e.g. `5D6+2` sword damage).

## Roll vs. Check (two different words)

- **Roll** = physically throw the die/dice to generate a random number.
- **Check** = place an experience check-mark in the box beside a Statistic, as a
  reminder to test it for improvement in the Winter Phase. See
  [[core.game-system.experience-checks]].

E.g. "Roll your Chaste Trait, and if you succeed, check it."

## Open vs. secret rolls

The default is to roll **in the open** (no script immunity — commit to random
results). The **exception** is Skills used for **inquiry** purposes (see Skill
Uses, p.95): the GM may roll these in secret and mislead players who fail,
withholding the check/Glory until after the encounter — and may even tell the
player to check the Skill on a failure, to preserve the illusion.

## Rounding

Values and dice outcomes round to the **nearest whole number**: a decimal of
0.1–0.4 is dropped; 0.5 or higher rounds up (3.4 → 3, 3.5 → 4).

## Quick Values (GM shortcut)

To make an opposed resolution with no Statistics at hand, roll **1D20 twice**: the
first roll *is* the Statistic's value, the second *is* the test. (Roll 8 then 12 =
"Dancing 8, and she failed.") Alternatively roll a suitable **`nD6 + modifier`** to
generate a value in a desired range (e.g. `2D6+8` for a Chaste value). Reserved for
interactions of little consequence — anything important deserves real Statistics.

title: The Critical Bonus (Statistics over 20)
text:
## The Critical Bonus

With the exception of **Characteristics**, no Statistic value may ever exceed 20.
Any points in a Skill, Trait, or Passion **above 20 become the critical bonus**,
written as `20 (+x)` where `x = value − 20`. The x-value is **always added to the
result of the d20 roll** for that Statistic.

Because the bonus is added to the roll, it **widens the critical range**: a
Statistic of `20 (+x)` scores a critical success on any natural roll **≥ 20 − x**.

- Example: a knight with **Sword 20 (+4)** who rolls 16 gets 16 + 4 = 20 — a
  critical. They critical on any roll **≥ 16**.
- So **Sword 22** is `20 (+2)`: it criticals on **18, 19, or 20**, and — being a
  value of 20 or more — **can never fail and can never fumble**.

The bonus also **improves opposed rolls even when the result is not a critical**,
since a higher roll beats a lower one.

**All criticals are equal.** A modified roll above 20 still counts simply as a
critical success with a value of **20**. If one combatant's modified roll is 21
and their opponent's is 30, both count as criticals of 20 — a **tie**.

### Temporary critical bonus from modifiers

Statistic modifiers or inspiration from Passions can create a **temporary**
critical bonus: if a modifier raises a value above 20, the difference over 20
becomes the bonus while it applies. E.g. Sword 18 with a +5 Height Advantage
becomes 23 → **20 (+3)** for as long as the advantage lasts.

### No fumble at 20+ (and its converse)

A **Statistic value of 20 has no chance of a fumble**; a natural 20 becomes a
**critical** instead (printed p.28). Thus a knight with Sword 16 (who normally
fumbles on a 20) who is bumped to **20 (+1)** by a +5 modifier can no longer
fumble. Conversely, a penalty that drops the effective value **below 20 makes
fumbles possible again**.

### Optional rule — mutual bonus reduction (opposed rolls)

When two characters make an opposed roll and **both** have a critical bonus,
reduce each bonus by the **lower** of the two. E.g. Sword `20 (+3)` vs `20 (+5)`
become `20` and `20 (+2)`. This puts equally-proficient characters on a more even
footing, yielding fewer criticals overall.

## Base outcomes (values ≤ 20, for context)

- **Critical:** natural roll exactly equals the Statistic value.
- **Success:** roll ≤ the value (roll-under).
- **Failure:** roll > the value.
- **Fumble:** a natural 20 — **unless** the value is 20+, in which case 20 is a
  critical and no fumble is possible.
- **Characteristics** are pass/fail only: no critical/fumble distinction, and
  they may exceed 20 (which simply means near-automatic success).

title: Experience Checks
text:
Every **Trait, Passion, and Skill** has a checkbox. Placing a **check** marks the
Statistic to make an **experience roll during the Winter Phase** (see Ch.14) to see
if the character improved. Checks are **not automatic** on any success — awarding or
denying them is one of the GM's key powers, and not all checks come from a roll.

## When a Player-knight should gain a check

- On a **critical success** (doing your best, learning is likely).
- On a **success under significant circumstances**.
- On a **fumble** (we learn from our greatest mistakes).

The GM may also grant checks for **player actions without any roll** — e.g. a player
who actually composes and sings a love song may be told to check **Compose** on GM
approval alone.

## Checking Traits & Passions without a roll

The GM may tell a player to check a **Trait or Passion** when the character has
displayed significant behavior in accordance with it — and it need not have been
witnessed by others. (A knight who lies to his lady about his fidelity might be told
to check **Deceitful**.)

title: The Glory Roll
text:
A **Glory Roll** is a roll against the character's **Glory ÷ 1,000** (rounded to the
nearest whole number). E.g. 3,755 Glory → roll **4 or less** to succeed
(3,755 ÷ 1,000 = 3.755 → 4).

It features most often at **feasts** (see [[gm.arthurian-acts.feasting]]), but two
knights may make an **opposed** Glory Roll to settle a minor social impasse at any
time.

title: Modifiers (Bonuses, Penalties, Reflexive) & Table 2.1
text:
Modifiers are **temporary** bonuses (up) or penalties (down) to **Statistic
values**. They always apply to the **Statistic, never to the die roll** — the only
thing ever added to a roll is the **critical bonus** (see
[[core.game-system.critical-bonus]]). The GM may grant or deny them at discretion.

## Values less than 1

A value reduced to **0 or below** counts simply as **0** (negative Statistics are
not used, except Hit Points in Ch.11). You still roll, and **failure is
automatic** — but the **fumble range widens by one point for every point below
zero**. E.g. Dancing 8 with a −10 modifier counts as 0 (not −2); its fumble range
becomes **18–20**.

## Table 2.1 — Skill Modifiers

| Nature of challenge | Modifier | When to use |
|--------------------|----------|-------------|
| Ordinary | +5 or −5 | Most situations |
| Strong | +10 or −10 | Dramatic situations |
| Extreme | +15 or −15 | Heroic situations |

Extreme is normally the largest, but **±20 (called Epic)** is possible on rare
occasions.

## Types of modifier

- **Trait & Passion modifiers** — applied when circumstances affect behavior/
  emotional state. All Trait modifiers are **reflexive**: a −10 Temperate is the
  same as +10 Indulgent. Players may request one when circumstances warrant; the
  recommended size is **+5 or −5**.
- **Characteristic modifiers** — usually penalties from external restriction (e.g.
  DEX −5 to sneak in a mail hauberk).
- **Damage modifiers** — add/subtract **dice** from damage: e.g. Weapon-Skill
  critical **+4D6**, unarmed Brawling critical **+2D6**, two-handed weapons
  **+2D6**, a bow **−1D6**. Some weapons instead modify the total rolled.
- **Skill modifiers** — make an action harder/easier (most combat modifiers are
  Skill modifiers based on weapon type, position, etc.). Use Table 2.1 for
  guidance.

## Reflexive modifiers (+X / −Y)

A reflexive modifier affects **both** values in an opposed resolution — a bonus to
one and a penalty to the other — written like **+5/−5** (a mounted knight gets +5
attacking a footman, who gets −5). Reflexive and other modifiers stack and may
cancel.

**A +5/−5 reflexive modifier is *not* the same as a single +10.** Example: Sword 15
vs 1H-Hafted 15 —
- With **+5/−5** → Sword 20 vs 1H-Hafted 10: the knight criticals 5% of the time,
  the knave succeeds (incl. partial) half the time.
- With a single **+10** → Sword 20 (+5) vs 1H-Hafted 15: the knight criticals 30%
  of the time, the knave succeeds three-quarters of the time.

title: Movement — Rate, Speed Multipliers & Overland Travel
text:
The average human **Movement Rate is 16** (1.6 yd/s, 3.2 mph); it equals
(STR + DEX) ÷ 2 + 5. In some Combat Actions the Movement Rate is used in an opposed
roll against an opponent's action (see [[core.combat.combat-movement]]).

## Table 2.2 — Speed Multipliers

| Bipeds | Quadrupeds |
|--------|-----------|
| Crawl ×¼ | — |
| Slow walk ×½ | Saunter ×½ |
| Walk ×1 | Walk ×1 |
| Jog ×2 | Trot ×2 |
| Run ×3 | Canter ×3 |
| — | Gallop ×6 |

## Table 2.3 — Modifiers to Movement Rate

Base Movement Rates assume an **armored knight**; adjust for lighter loads:

| Encumbrance | Modifier |
|-------------|----------|
| Unencumbered | +4 |
| Weapons and shield only | +3 |
| Non-metal armor | +2 |
| Metal armor | no bonus or penalty |

## Overland movement

On royal roads both horsed and unhorsed characters cover **~20 miles/day** (castles
and market towns sit ~20 miles apart), assuming a known/guided way, supplied food,
suitable weather, a maintained road, and nothing unusual. For leisurely travel a
party moves at the pace of its **slowest** member, so individual Movement Rates
don't matter. Riding faster risks a horse blowing its wind (never recovered); the
usual fast long-distance pace is trot, trot, then canter at 15-minute intervals.

### Types of travel

- **Exploring** — tense slow walk, watching for danger/surprise.
- **Leisurely** — easy slow walk (ladies, siege trains, merchants, injured needing
  Chirurgery).
- **Normal** — trot/walk/canter intervals; usual knightly pace.
- **Hurried or Forced March** — intentionally fast, **dangerous for horses**. At the
  march's end roll against the horse's **CON**:
  - **Critical** — completes, *plus* half the horse's Movement Rate in extra miles.
  - **Success** — completes the distance.
  - **Failure** — exhaustion: moves **half** distance and can go no faster than
    Leisurely until it has rested a day.
  - **Fumble** — serious horse injury; a new steed is needed.

### Types of road & weather

- **Roads** — *Roman* (ancient paved, usually unmaintained but serviceable),
  *Trade* (raised dirt/gravel, repaired regularly), *Local* (undrained, ill-repaired
  dirt), *Path* (narrow marked trail).
- **Weather** — *Good* (warm, at most light rain), *Bad* (heavy rain, mud, wind,
  flooded fords), *Terrible* (snow, ice, frozen/uncertain roads).

## Table 2.4 — Overland Daily Riding Rate (miles/day)

Without a guide or foreknowledge; no wheeled vehicles (with wheels, never faster
than Leisurely).

| Weather & road conditions | Exploring | Leisurely | Normal | Hurried/Forced |
|---------------------------|-----------|-----------|--------|----------------|
| Good on Trade road, or Good/Bad on Roman road | 5 | 15 | 20 | 30 |
| Good on Local, or Bad on Trade, or Terrible on Roman | 4 | 10 | 15 | 25 |
| Good on Path | 2 | 5 | 8 | 12 |
| Bad on Local road | 3 | 7½ | 10 | 15 |
| Bad on Path | 1 | 4 | 5 | 7½ |
| Terrible on Trade road | 3 | 7½ | 10 | 15 |
| Terrible on Local road | 1 | 4 | 5 | 7½ |
| Terrible on Path | ½ | 1 | 1½ | 2 |

Full competitive-movement rules are under **Races and Chases** in the GM Handbook.
Maps are exceedingly rare; a written list of stops (manor/castle/monastery/city, or
a landholder's coat of arms if illiterate) commonly replaces them.

title: Resolution — Unopposed, Opposed & Fixed
text:
A single **roll-under d20 mechanic** resolves every action. Most things a
character does succeed automatically and need no roll — you roll only when an
action requires skill/discipline under stress, scrutiny, or haste, or when an
outside force acts on the character.

## Unopposed resolution — four outcomes

Roll 1D20 directly against the pertinent Statistic value:

- **Critical success** — roll **exactly equals** the (modified) value. The
  ultimate success, with extra benefits; always warrants a **check** to a Trait,
  Passion, or Skill, and sometimes grants extra Glory. Always compare against the
  *final modified* value (Skill 6 with +5 → 11: an 11 now criticals, a 6 is just a
  success).
- **Success** — roll **less than** the value. If significant, the GM *may* grant a
  check (not automatic just because a roll was made).
- **Failure** — roll **greater than** the value. The action fails / the Trait or
  Passion is not activated.
- **Fumble** — a **natural 20**, *unless* the value is 20 (then 20 is a critical
  and no fumble is possible). A disastrous stroke of bad luck (drop/break a weapon,
  cough mid-ballad). GM's option: a fumble may call for a check — we learn from our
  worst mistakes. A fumble is not a licence for the GM to inflict endless grief.

**Characteristics** are pass/fail only: no critical/fumble distinction and no
checks.

## Opposed resolution — five outcomes

Made like an unopposed roll but compared against another roll (an opponent's
Statistic or a fixed value). To **win** you must both succeed *and* roll higher
than the opponent.

- **Win** — succeed (roll ≤ value) and roll higher than the opponent. A **critical
  beats any non-critical** and guarantees at least a tie — even a value-1 character
  rolling a 1 wins, since all criticals are equal.
- **Loss** — roll greater than your value (both parties can lose). A **fumbled**
  loss adds insult to injury (in combat, you drop/break your weapon).
- **Partial success** — you succeed (roll < value) but roll **lower** than the
  opponent. Usually a minor benefit (in combat, you still get your Shield/Parry
  Protection).
- **Tie** — both succeed and roll the **same** number. Critical values are never
  counted for size, so if **both critical, it is a tie**. In combat a tie means
  both strike (with exceptions — see Ch.7).
- **Mutual failure** — both fail; nothing happens, situation unresolved.

### Friendly opposed resolution

When several players roll the same Skill/Trait, the **highest successful** result
wins the contest; only that winner receives a check.

## Fixed opposition

Against passive resistance (break a door, resist a poison), roll opposed against a
**fixed value**. The roll must succeed *and* beat that value — so a character whose
Statistic is ≤ the fixed value can only win on a **critical**. (A door of value 15
needs a STR roll that succeeds and beats 15.)

title: Horsemanship (Skill) + fumbling a Horsemanship roll
text:
## Horsemanship (Skill)

- **Categories:** Combat, Knightly, Ladies
- **Use:** Deed, Inquiry
- **Glory:** No

Feudal society is an equine society: horses are central to a knight's existence.
**All noble men and women have this Skill** and begin learning it young, so
**riding at any pace requires no roll** under ordinary conditions.

A Horsemanship roll is called for only in **difficult circumstances**, such as:
- Jumping ditches and hedges
- Racing, chasing, or covering long distances at speed
- Horse care and tending to unusual circumstances
- Riding side-saddle at a trot, canter, or gallop
- Appraising a horse's value, outfitting it properly, and anything else
  associated with horses
- **Contests** where competitors try to outdo each other, even in ordinary
  equine affairs

As an **Inquiry** skill it also supplies knowledge: e.g. to figure out the breed
of a horse, roll Horsemanship.

**Not for training horses** — that is a separate Skill outside a knight's or
lady's knowledge.

## Fumbling a Horsemanship roll

### General (Deed) fumble — printed p. 95
Horsemanship is a **Deed** skill (e.g. riding through difficult terrain). The
general resolution outcomes apply:
- **Failure:** the character does not accomplish the deed.
- **Fumble:** the character does not accomplish the deed **and takes an
  experience check** to the Skill. The Gamemaster **may impose a negative
  modifier** to a follow-up resolution of relevant Traits, Passions, or Skills
  (e.g. a botched jump that scatters the hunt, unseats the rider, or spooks the
  horse into the next roll).

The specific bad thing that happens on a fumble is left to the GM and the
situation; falling from the mount, injuring the horse, or losing a race are
typical.

### Combat-specific fumbles
When Horsemanship is rolled inside the combat system, the dedicated fumble
entries govern the result instead of the generic Deed rule:
- **Control Mount** fumble → rider is **thrown** (see [[core.combat.mounted-utility-actions]]).
- **Emergency Dismount** fumble → **2D6** damage, drop all weapons; a falling
  horse lands on the rider (Table 7.4, see [[core.combat.mounted-combat]]).
- **Mounted Lance Charge** fumble → Table 7.2 consequences (see
  [[core.combat.action-mounted-charge]]).

title: Afflictions — Madness, Melancholy & Misery
text:
Afflictions arise from certain failed Passion rolls (see the Passion Crisis). All can
be cured.

## Madness

A Maddened character is **Out of Game** — throws away weapons/armor, flees into the
wilderness (or collapses catatonic); the player hands the sheet to the GM and runs a
**Madness Solo** each Winter Phase while raving.

- **Glory:** 100 if it lasts a year or more, otherwise 25.
- **Curing:** only by someone who **Loves/Adores** the character, someone the character
  holds a Loyalty/Love/Adoration for, a **Famous/Exalted Merciful** person, a
  healing-professional monk/lady/hermit, or the **Holy Grail**. The healer succeeds a
  **Merciful** roll to calm them, then shelters and visits daily — **each month of care
  removes one year** of Madness duration; at 0 the mind clears (usually no memory of
  the episode). Madness lasting **under a month** must resolve on its own. Some
  enchanted wells/miracles/the Grail cure instantly.
- **Out-of-Game curing:** the GM may return the sheet at any time (adjusting Statistics
  to reflect the episode) — handy when the active character dies or goes Mad.

## Melancholy

A depressed state: **−5 to all Skill and Passion rolls**; incapable of normal action.

- **Glory:** 10. Effects wait until any current activity (e.g. a battle) finishes.
- **Value/duration:** equals a number of days (per Passion strength); left alone the
  **value drops 1/day**, then the character recovers. This value is the fixed
  opposition against a cure.
- **Friendly Cure:** someone with a Love/Loyalty/Adoration bond makes an **opposed
  Passion roll vs the Melancholy value** — win = lifted; partial = value −1, retry
  tomorrow; lose = the knight turns **violent** (→ Unfriendly Cure).
- **Unfriendly Cure:** being attacked snaps them out to defend themselves; combat (or a
  monk/lady's verbal assault/slap via a Cruel roll) continues until the healer is hurt
  or flees, or the Melancholic takes damage (which **ends** the affliction). One cure
  attempt per person per day.

## Misery

- **Becoming Miserable:** whenever an **Adoration** roll is failed (plus its other
  effects); or when Adoration is invoked away from the Beloved after Inspiration passes
  (if Impassioned via a critical, become **Melancholic** instead); the GM may also
  apply it on loss of a Love/Loyalty source. **Glory:** 10 (first time each year).
- **Effect:** **−2 to all Skills and Passions** until dispelled (stacks with other
  penalties).
- **Duration:** from a failed Adoration roll → ends 7 days after the following Sunday
  (or when cured); from loss of a loved one → weeks equal to the Passion's value.
- **Curing:** another person disturbs them with a successful **opposed Skill/Passion
  roll** (Intrigue, Orate; Merciful, Trusting; Homage, Loyalty (Companions), Chivalry,
  Duty (Vassals)) vs the causing Passion; a failed attempt triggers a
  Melancholy-style violent reaction. Also cured by seeing/hearing the Beloved.

title: Directed Traits & Obsessions (Avarice, Fear, Jealousy — Table 4.1)
text:
## Directed Traits

A **Directed Trait** is a feeling focused on a person/group that overrides the general
attitude. Mark the Trait with an asterisk and note the object + modifier, e.g.
`*Suspicious (King Mark) +5`. When rolling that Trait about its object, add the
modifier **and reduce the opposing Trait by the same amount** (Trusting 14/Suspicious
6 becomes Trusting 9/Suspicious 11 vs King Mark).

- **Inherited:** starts at **half the parent's** value.
- **Voluntary:** usually **+1D6** (or as agreed).
- **GM-assigned:** usually **not more than +5**.
- **Raising:** with a check, roll higher than the current value in the Winter Phase to
  increase it by 1.

## Obsessions

A stronger Directed Trait that **always** affects actions. An **Obsession roll** is
made each time the character encounters or hears about its object. Obsessions arise
from unlucky rolls, GM ruling, or player request.

**Redemption:** (1) reduce it in the Winter Phase like a Passion; or (2) in the
object's presence, make an **opposed Honor vs Obsession** roll (Table 4.1). An
overweening Obsession can also be escaped by retiring to a monastery/hermitage
(Out of Game for good).

### Table 4.1 — Obsession Resolution Results (Honor vs Obsession)

| Result | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Critical | Overcome it — remove from sheet |
| Win | Partly overcome — **halve** its value |
| Tie | Attempt another opposed roll, or not (player's option) |
| Partial success | Reduce by 1 point |
| Loss | Waxes stronger — value **increases by half** |
| Fumble | Impossible to overcome — value **doubles** |

## The named Obsessions

- **Avarice** (extreme Selfish) — start **+2D6** to Selfish. Paths: fumble a Generous
  roll then succeed Selfish; **or** gain a Selfish critical bonus (GM picks the
  object). Effects: lacking the object causes **Misery** (once/day, crit or success →
  Misery); when a chance to obtain it arises, a Passion-style roll compels acquisition
  (critical = at any cost, morality aside).
- **Fear** (extreme Cowardly) — start **+1D6+5** to Cowardly. Paths: fumble a Valorous
  roll then succeed Cowardly; **or** GM/player decision. Effect: when confronted by the
  object, an unopposed Fear roll — success = refuse/withdraw to safety; critical = flee
  in terror at max rate until exhausted. Saves lives but costs Honor when fleeing is
  unbecoming.
- **Jealousy** (extreme Suspicious) — start **+2D6** to Suspicious. Paths include:
  fumble a Trusting roll then succeed Suspicious; fumble an obligatory Adoration roll;
  being publicly rebuffed by one's Adored (automatic); resentment of betters; Romantic
  Lovers must acquire a Jealousy of any threat to their Beloved. Effect: must try to
  **harm the Rival** (physically, socially, or via a Skill contest). In the Rival's
  company: **−5 to Forgiving, Just, Merciful, Prudent, Spiritual, and Trusting**.

title: The Passion Roll — Inspiration, Impassionment & Passion Crisis (Table 4.2)
text:
Most Passion rolls are **unopposed**. Each Passion may be used to **provoke a bonus
only once per day** (rolls made purely to decide a course of action don't count
against this limit).

## Table 4.2 — Unopposed Passion Roll Results

| Result | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Critical** | **Impassioned** — gain a check |
| **Success** | **Inspired** — gain a check |
| **Failure** | **Passion Crisis** (see below) |
| **Fumble** | Lose 1 point from the Passion |

- **Impassioned:** **+10** to a single Skill or Trait (player's choice) until the
  evoking situation ends (a duel until someone drops; a battle Skill bonus lasts one
  Battle Turn; may modify a series of First Aid/Chirurgery rolls from one trauma).
- **Inspired:** **+5** to a single Skill or Trait while the situation persists.

**Modifying Traits with Passions:** the Inspired/Impassioned bonus can be applied to a
**Trait** to improve (or, by boosting an Unsung Trait, deliberately lower a Famous/
Exalted) Trait roll.

## Passion Crisis ("For Dole and Sorrow")

Triggered by a **failed** Table 4.2 roll — or when a character Inspired/Impassioned
fails spectacularly at the task, or the Passion's source is lost/removed forever.
Make an **unopposed roll against the triggering Passion** (+ modifiers):

- **Critical success → Madness** · **Success → Melancholy** · **Failure → no effect**
  · **Fumble → lose 1 point** from the Passion.

**Modifiers to that roll:** failed while Inspired **+0**; failed while Impassioned
**+5**; currently Inspired by it **+5**; crisis due to own action/inaction **+10**;
currently Impassioned by it **+10**.

**Affliction duration** (by unmodified Passion level):

| Level | Melancholic | Maddened |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Unsung (1–4) | 1D6 hours | one week |
| Normal (5–15) | one day | 1D6 weeks |
| Famous (16–20) | 1D6 days | 1D6 months |
| Exalted (20+x) | 1D6 weeks | 1D6 years |

(Both may be healed before the duration ends — see [[core.traits-passions.afflictions]].)

## Internal Conflict

Passions may be used in **opposed** rolls to resolve inner conflict — usually a
Passion vs a Trait. The player rolls both; the winner decides the action. (E.g. Hate
(Saxons) 18 vs Merciful 12 over sparing civilians.)

title: Passions of Fervor, Adoratio & Civilitas (Love/Hate, Adoration/Devotion, Chivalry/Hospitality/Station)
text:
## Fervor — Love & Hate

Opposites; you cannot hold **both** Love and Hate for the same subject (though
Hate (Cornishmen) + Love (Tristram the Cornishman) is fine). Their bonuses apply only
to matters concerning the subject.

- **Hate (Person/Group)** — invoked on mere **awareness of proximity** (no contact
  needed), making Exalted Hates dangerous in peaceful settings. Choose the subject
  carefully — too broad brings constant grief, too narrow is useless. Restraint =
  opposed Hate vs another Passion/Trait (Homage, Chivalry; or Forgiving/Just/Merciful/
  Trusting).
- **Love (Family)** — a **Universal Passion** every character has; invoked when family
  is endangered. (Family = immediate blood/adopted; Kin = extended; Lineage = common
  ancestor; Clan = close-knit related families.)
- **Love (Person)** — a tender/physical bond gained in play (GM may impose it). It is
  also the **successor to Adoration** once consummated, keeping the same value. Invoked
  when the subject is in danger.

## Adoratio — Adoration & Devotion
